## Outline agreed with the user (follow it strictly)
One-Factor-at-a-Time Hyperparameter Tuning of YOLOv8 Training Variables for Reliable Fruit Ripeness Detection

Problem Statement and Contribution  
Manual or default selection of training data hyperparameters (input resolution, augmentation, batch size, learning rate) often leads to suboptimal fruit ripeness detection with YOLO models. This study systematically examines, via an OFAT (One Factor At a Time) protocol, the isolated impact of each training hyperparameter on YOLOv8n performance for a multi-class banana ripeness task. The contribution is a prioritised set of tuning guidelines and an optimised configuration that improves mAP@0.5 by ≥8% over baseline, enabling robust deployment in agricultural sorting.

Methodology  
A custom dataset of 3,000 overhead banana images (1,000 per class: unripe green, ripe yellow, overripe brown) is captured under controlled lighting at 1920×1080 resolution. A YOLOv8n detector is trained in PyTorch on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090. OFAT experiments vary one hyperparameter while others are fixed at defaults (YOLOv8’s standard training recipe). Explored hyperparameters and levels: input size (416, 640, 832 pixels), batch size (16, 32, 64), mosaic augmentation probability (0.5, 0.8, 1.0), mixup probability (0.0, 0.2, 0.5), initial learning rate (0.01, 0.001 with cosine annealing), and epochs (100, 200, 300). Each run uses a fixed 70%-20%-10% stratified split, identical seed, and early stopping on validation mAP. The best model is selected by peak validation mAP@0.5.

Experimental Setup  
All 18 OFAT runs use identical hardware and software environment. Training time per run ranges from 2.5 to 6 hours depending on input size and epochs. Metrics evaluated on the held-out test set: mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, precision, recall, and per-class average precision (AP). A baseline model using all default YOLOv8n settings (640 px, batch 16, mosaic 1.0, no mixup, lr 0.01, 300 epochs) is compared against the best OFAT configuration.

Expected Result Figures and Tables  
1. Table: Full OFAT results—each hyperparameter level with mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, precision, recall.  
2. Figure: Line graph of mAP@0.5 vs. input resolution (416, 640, 832) showing an optimal point.  
3. Bar chart comparing test mAP for best configuration vs. baseline, with error bars over 5 replicates.

In this study, we extensively evaluated the viability of the state-of-the-art YOLOv8 architecture for object detec-
tion tasks, speciﬁcally tailored for smoke and wildﬁre identiﬁcation with a focus on agricultural and environmen-
tal safety. All available versions of YOLOv8 were initially ﬁne-tuned on a domain-speciﬁc dataset that included a
variety of scenarios, crucial for comprehensive agricultural monitoring. The ‘large’ version (YOLOv8l) was se-
lected for further hyperparameter tuning based on its performance metrics. This model underwent a detailed
hyperparameter optimization using the One Factor At a Time (OFAT) methodology, concentrating on key param-
eters such as learning rate, batch size, weight decay, epochs, and optimizer. Insights from the OFAT study were
used to deﬁne search spaces for a subsequent Random Search (RS). The ﬁnal model derived from RS demon-
strated signiﬁcant improvements over the initial ﬁne-tuned model, increasing overall precision by 1.39 %, recall
by 1.48 %, F1-score by 1.44 %, mAP@0.50 by 0.70 %, and mAP@0.50:0.95 by 5.09 %. We validated the enhanced
model's efﬁcacy on a diverse set of real-world images, reﬂecting various agricultural settings, to conﬁrm its ro-
bustness in detecting smoke and ﬁre. These results underscore the model's reliability and effectiveness in scenar-
ios critical to agricultural safety and environmental monitoring. This work, representing a signiﬁcant
advancement in the ﬁeld of ﬁre and smoke detection through machine learning, lays a strong foundation for fu-
ture research and solutions aimed at safeguarding agricultural areas and natural environments.

tions in food supply chains.
The repercussions of wildﬁres on agriculture extend beyond the im-
mediate devastation. They result in the loss of vegetation cover which is
vital for soil health and fertility, leading to increased soil erosion and re-
duced agricultural productivity Girona-García et al. (2023); Paul et al.
(2022). The smoke from these ﬁres also adversely affects air quality,
which can have direct negative impacts on crop yields and livestock
health, further exacerbating the challenges faced by farmers and agri-
businesses Jaffe et al. (2020).
Moreover, wildﬁres disrupt local ecosystems and biodiversity, which
are essential for sustainable agricultural practices. The loss of ﬂora and
fauna due to ﬁres can lead to imbalances in agricultural ecosystems, af-
fecting pollination, pest control, and other natural services crucial for
crop productionAlbery et al. (2021).
In this critical context, timely detection and monitoring of wildﬁres
are paramount, albeit challenging tasks that demand robust technolog-
ical solutions Khan et al. (2020). Early wildﬁre detection is not only
crucial for saving lives and minimizing property damage but also plays
a vital role in protecting agricultural resources and maintaining food
security.
Traditional wildﬁre detection methods have been foundational in
early warning strategies. However, these methods come with signiﬁ-
cant limitations. Human observation is constrained by visibility and
the potential for human error, making it unreliable for 24/7 monitoring
Casas, Ramos et al. (2024). Sensor-based systems, while offering auto-
mated surveillance, are prone to false alarms from non-ﬁre sources

These challenges highlight the need for integrating advanced tech-

management to overcome the inherent limitations of traditional
methods and enhance the effectiveness of detection systems Kinaneva

In the ﬁeld of AI, speciﬁcally in computer vision (CV), various ap-
proaches have been explored for the identiﬁcation of wildﬁres and
smoke. Among these, segmentation techniques are particularly useful,
enabling the precise delineation of ﬁre and smoke contours in images,
which facilitates accurate monitoring and assessment of affected areas
Khryashchev and Larionov (2020). Within this group of approaches, fa-
mous architectures like Mask-RCNN and Faster-RCNN have been noted
for their effectiveness Qurratulain et al. (2023).
However, object detection has become the most utilized technique
in this ﬁeld due to its ability to quickly and accurately identify ﬁre and
smoke instances in diverse environments. Within this category, re-
nowned architectures like ResNet and VGG are some of the most well-
known and widely used Reis and Turk (2023). Yet, the You Only Look
Once (YOLO) architecture has emerged as a cornerstone for real-time
object detection.
YOLO has become a staple for real-time object detection Jiang et al.
(2022). Its uniqueness resides in its single-shot detection approach,
contrasting sharply with two-stage (two-shot) detection methods.
Single-shot object detection streamlines the detection process by mak-
ing predictions about the location of objects in a single pass through the
input image Jin et al. (2020). This computational efﬁciency is particu-
larly advantageous in scenarios where rapid response is critical, such
as in the detection of wildﬁres.
In comparison, two-shot detection methods, such as Mask R-CNN,
operate in a more complex process. The initial pass generates a set of
proposals for potential object locations, and a subsequent pass reﬁnes
these proposals to make ﬁnal predictions Jin et al. (2020); Yang et al.
(2021). This method is more computationally demanding due to the
dual processing stages required for detection, making it less efﬁcient
for applications where rapid response is essential.
Usually, two-shot methods were considered more accurate due to
their detailed proposal reﬁnement process Li et al. (2023). However, ad-
vancements in CV have signiﬁcantly narrowed this gap. The advance-
ment in this area has led to the development of single-shot
architectures with precision that rivals their two-shot counterparts.
A prime example of this progress is seen in the YOLO architecture se-
ries, which has demonstrated continuous improvement in accuracy
with each iteration. These enhancements have solidiﬁed YOLO's posi-
tion as a highly effective tool for applications demanding both speed
and precision, making it an optimal choice for real-time challenges
like wildﬁre detection.
The evolution of YOLO has led to the development of YOLOv8 Jocher
et al., 2023, one of the most recent and advanced variants of the archi-
tecture. With ﬁve distinct versions, each tailored for varying balances
of performance and efﬁciency, YOLOv8 brings a new level of adaptabil-
ity to object detection.
Based on the above, this research explores the potential of YOLOv8
as a promising tool for real-time smoke and wildﬁre detection. The em-
phasis of our study is on the critical application within agricultural set-
tings, where the swift identiﬁcation of such threats is vital to
safeguarding crops and livelihoods from the devastating impact of
wildﬁres.
This research methodology initiates with ﬁne-tuning YOLOv8's ﬁve
pre-trained variants on a dataset tailored for smoke and wildﬁre detec-
tion, employing metrics like precision, recall, f1-score, and mAP to
determine the most effective variant, emphasizing recall for its
signiﬁcance in emergency scenarios. The leading model then undergoes
hyperparameter optimization, starting with a One Factor at a Time anal-
ysis to evaluate individual parameter impacts, followed by a targeted
random search to ﬁne-tune the settings, streamlining the model's per-
formance for optimal real-time detection.
As a result, we have achieved an optimized model that shows im-
provements across all metrics. Furthermore, visual tests corroborate
the quantitative improvements, showing the model's superior perfor-
mance in detecting instances of ﬁre and smoke in diverse conditions
more consistently and accurately.
This study seeks to contribute to the urgent and ever-evolving ﬁeld
of wildﬁre detection. By leveraging state-of-the-art technology to ad-
dress this globally pressing concern, it underscores the vital role of con-
tinuous innovation and research in the face of mounting environmental
challenges.
2. Methods
2.1. Dataset
The Fire And Smoke dataset Naseer (2022), central to this research,
is publicly available on the Roboﬂow platform. Comprised of a diverse
collection of 9796 images, this dataset offers an extensive exploration
of smoke and wildﬁre phenomena in various conditions and perspec-
tives, as shown in Fig. 1. The dataset is partitioned into three subsets
to facilitate the training and evaluation of the models: 6856 images for
training, 1963 for validation, and 977 for testing.
What sets the Fire And Smoke dataset apart is its diversity in repre-
senting the complexity of real-world scenarios. The images encapsulate
different luminous conditions, providing insights into how smoke and
ﬁre appear under varying lighting. These variations challenge the
models' ability to detect critical features, which are crucial for early de-
tection and timely response.
Furthermore, the dataset includes photographs taken from different
perspectives and distances, ranging from close-up views to distant ob-
servations. This variety helps in training the models to recognize wild-
ﬁres and smoke across different scales and angles, enhancing their
applicability across a wide range of scenarios. The inclusion of images
with occlusion adds another layer of complexity, mimicking the chal-
lenges faced in real-world detection where objects might obstruct the
view.
The heterogeneity of the Fire And Smoke dataset, in terms of light-
ing, scene conditions, perspectives, and occlusions, presents a robust
and realistic challenge. Such a comprehensive and varied dataset is
instrumental in ﬁne-tuning the ﬁve variants of YOLOv8 for the intri-
cate task of smoke and wildﬁre detection. It allows the research to
not only evaluate the performance under controlled conditions but
also assess how well the models might perform in the varied and
unpredictable circumstances that characterize real-world wildﬁre
events.
Crucially, the selection of the Fire And Smoke dataset was guided
by its inclusion of images depicting wildﬁre and smoke occurrences
not only in agricultural zones but also in various other settings such
as forests, mountainous regions, and human-made structures like
houses and vehicles. This comprehensive range is particularly relevant
for agricultural safety, as wildﬁres often originate or spread from
these diverse sources. A ﬁre starting in a nearby forest, residential
area, or from an automotive cause can quickly escalate and spread to
farmlands, making early detection in these varied scenarios just as
critical.
By training the models with this diverse dataset, the research ac-
knowledges the interconnected nature of agricultural and surrounding
environments, emphasizing the need for a detection system that is vig-
ilant across a spectrum of possible ignition points and pathways. This
approach ensures that the YOLOv8 models are not exclusively trained
to detect ﬁres in areas with crops or typical agricultural terrains. Instead,

Building upon the success of YOLOv5, YOLOv8 introduces a series of

that enhance both efﬁciency and adaptability, making YOLOv8 a stand-

A noteworthy innovation in YOLOv8 is its transition from an anchor-
box approach to anchor-free detection Vats and Anastasiu (2023). This
alteration enables more direct object center predictions, simplifying
the Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) process and overcoming previ-
ous challenges related to generalization and irregular handling
Dumitriu et al. (2023); Casas et al. (2023).
The structural improvements extend further, with reﬁnements to
the convolutional design. Notably, YOLOv8 replaces the initial 6 × 6 con-
volution with a more efﬁcient 3 × 3, while introducing C2f in place of C3
Casas et al. (2023); Ramos et al. (2024). These modiﬁcations provide a
streamlined and versatile model structure, contributing to a more effec-
tive and robust design.
An addition of the Spatial Pyramid Pooling Feature (SPPF)
strengthens the model's ability to detect objects across different scales
Vats and Anastasiu (2023); Ramos et al. (2024). Moreover, the concate-
nation of features directly within the model's neck, along with the new
mosaic augmentation technique during training, adds to the model's
ﬂexibility and efﬁciency Doan Van (2023); Casas et al. (2023).
Loss is a key aspect in the optimization of YOLOv8, as it is used to
quantify the difference between the predicted outputs of the model
and the actual or expected values. YOLOv8 employs a combination of
box loss, classiﬁcation (cls) loss, and distributional focal loss (dﬂ). The
signiﬁcance of each of these losses and their role in the model's perfor-
mance is explained below:
• Box loss: Measuring the discrepancy between predicted bounding
box coordinates and ground truth Wang et al. (2020a), Casas et al.
(2023), using metrics like mean squared error (MSE) or smooth L1
loss.
• Classiﬁcation (cls) loss: Quantifying the disparity between predicted
class probabilities and true labels (Wu et al., 2022), Casas et al. (2023),
utilizing categorical cross-entropy loss.
• Distributional focal loss (dﬂ): An extension of focal loss, handling
class imbalance in object detection Li et al. (2020); Casas et al.
(2023) by assigning higher weights to harder-to-classify examples.
YOLOv8 comes in various sizes, including nano (YOLOv8n), small

(YOLOv8x) versions. In this research, we are analyzing all ﬁve versions,

Abstract: Apple grading is an essential part of the apple marketing process to achieve high proﬁts.
In this paper, an improved YOLOv5 apple grading method is proposed to address the problems of
low grading accuracy and slow grading speed in the apple grading process and is experimentally
veriﬁed by the designed automatic apple grading machine. Firstly, the Mish activation function is
used instead of the original YOLOv5 activation function, which allows the apple feature information
to ﬂow in the deep network and improves the generalization ability of the model. Secondly, the
distance intersection overUnion loss function (DIoU_Loss) is used to speed up the border regression
rate and improve the model convergence speed. In order to reﬁne the model to focus on apple
feature information, a channel attention module (Squeeze Excitation) was added to the YOLOv5
backbone network to enhance information propagation between features and improve the model’s
ability to extract fruit features. The experimental results show that the improved YOLOv5 algorithm
achieves an average accuracy of 90.6% for apple grading under the test set, which is 14.8%, 11.1%,
and 3.7% better than the SSD, YOLOv4, and YOLOv5s models, respectively, with a real-time grading
frame rate of 59.63 FPS. Finally, the improved YOLOv5 apple grading algorithm is experimentally
validated on the developed apple auto-grader. The improved YOLOv5 apple grading algorithm was
experimentally validated on the developed apple auto grader. The experimental results showed that
the grading accuracy of the automatic apple grader reached 93%, and the grading speed was four
apples/sec, indicating that this method has a high grading speed and accuracy for apples, which is of
practical signiﬁcance for advancing the development of automatic apple grading.

1. Introduction
Today, labour on farms and orchards relies heavily on manual labour by skilled farm-
ers, which can lead to increased time and production costs. Smart farming has become
a popular concept with the development of precision farming and information technol-
ogy [1]. China is a major apple-producing country globally, and apple sorting has a high
economic application value [2]. With increased economic development, people have higher
requirements for fruit quality [3,4]. As a critical element in improving apple quality and
liberating orchard labour, apple grading technology is of great signiﬁcance in increasing
the added value of products, improving market competitiveness, and alleviating labour
shortages in orchards. Therefore, a high precision and speed grading method is needed for
the effective and objective grading of apples.
In the research of fruit grading based on traditional machine learning, Abdullah et al. [5]
detected the quality features of poppy peaches by machine learning, the features considered
mainly included fruit surface color and fruit shape, and developed automatic machine vi-
sion detection software to detect the ripeness grade of poppy peaches by linear discriminant
analysis and multilayer neural network. Marchant et al. [6] studied the method of auto-
matic potato detection and grading based on a computer vision system. Moallem et al. [7]

In the above machine learning classiﬁcation methods, preprocessing of images is often

In the research of fruit grading based on deep learning, Fan et al. [9] used a con-

on length: small, medium, large and extra large, where the accuracy of the ResNet deep
learning model reached over 99%. Luna et al. [11] proposed a deep learning-based method
for single tomato defect area detection, implemented through the OpenCV library and
Python programming. He collected 1200 tomato images of different qualities using an
image capture box and used the images for training VGG16, InceptionV3, and ResNet50
deep learning models, respectively, compared the experimental results and found that
VGG16 was the best deep learning model for defect recognition. However, there are still
problems of insufﬁcient model optimization and poor real-time performance in the above
deep learning model grading methods.
In terms of research on automatic fruit grading equipment, Cubero et al. [12] designed
a computer vision-based automated citrus sorting device. The sorting device was deployed
on a mobile platform, and the low-power industrial camera image acquisition and powerful
lighting system enabled the device to work better in the ﬁeld. Experiments showed that the
sorting device could achieve a sorting speed of up to eight per second. Baigvand et al. [13]
developed a machine learning-based ﬁg sorting system, which ﬁrst uses a feeder and a belt.
The ﬁgs were ﬁrst transported under a CCD camera by a feeder and belt conveyor. The ﬁgs
were classiﬁed into ﬁve categories by extracting ﬁg characteristics from the pictures taken
by the CCD camera, including size, colour, segmentation size and ﬁg centre position, etc.
The experiments veriﬁed that the grading system was 95% accurate in recognizing the ﬁve
categories of ﬁgs. However, the designed automatic fruit grader tends to be large and more
suitable for large assembly line working modes and is not suitable for the needs of small
and medium-sized farmers for detection and grading.
Although the above methods have achieved speciﬁc results in terms of fruit feature
detection and equipment implementation, there are still problems, such as insufﬁcient
model optimization and equipment implementation. Based on this, this paper takes red
Fuji apples as the research object. It provides an in-depth discussion on the grading
detection of apple features and the implementation of automatic apple sorting equipment.
An apple grading algorithm based on the improved YOLOv5 is proposed, using the Mish
activation function instead of the original Relu activation function to improve the model
generalization ability. A loss function (DIou_Loss) is introduced to speed up the rate of
edge regression and improve localization accuracy. The attention mechanism squeeze
excitation (SE) module is embedded into the backbone feature network to improve the
feature extraction ability of the model. Experimental results show that the improved method
can improve the model detection without increasing the model training cost. Finally, the
automatic apple grader designed based on this paper was experimentally validated, and
some conclusions were obtained.

Object Detection With Deep Learning: A Review
Zhong-Qiu Zhao
, Member, IEEE, Peng Zheng, Shou-Tao Xu, and Xindong Wu
, Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—Due to object detection’s close relationship with
video analysis and image understanding, it has attracted much
research attention in recent years. Traditional object detection
methods are built on handcrafted features and shallow trainable
architectures. Their performance easily stagnates by construct-
ing complex ensembles that combine multiple low-level image
features with high-level context from object detectors and scene
classiﬁers. With the rapid development in deep learning, more
powerful tools, which are able to learn semantic, high-level,
deeper features, are introduced to address the problems existing
in traditional architectures. These models behave differently in
network architecture, training strategy, and optimization func-
tion. In this paper, we provide a review of deep learning-based
object detection frameworks. Our review begins with a brief
introduction on the history of deep learning and its representative
tool, namely, the convolutional neural network. Then, we focus
on typical generic object detection architectures along with some
modiﬁcations and useful tricks to improve detection performance
further. As distinct speciﬁc detection tasks exhibit different
characteristics, we also brieﬂy survey several speciﬁc tasks,
including salient object detection, face detection, and pedestrian
detection. Experimental analyses are also provided to compare
various methods and draw some meaningful conclusions. Finally,
several promising directions and tasks are provided to serve as
guidelines for future work in both object detection and relevant
neural network-based learning systems.
Index Terms—Deep learning, neural network, object detection.

The problem deﬁnition of object detection is to determine
where objects are located in a given image (object localization)
and which category each object belongs to (object classiﬁca-
tion). Therefore, the pipeline of traditional object detection
models can be mainly divided into three stages: informative
region selection, feature extraction, and classiﬁcation.
A. Informative Region Selection
As different objects may appear in any positions of the
image and have different aspect ratios or sizes, it is a natural
choice to scan the whole image with a multiscale sliding
window. Although this exhaustive strategy can ﬁnd out all
possible positions of the objects, its shortcomings are also
obvious. Due to a large number of candidate windows, it is
computationally expensive and produces too many redundant
windows. However, if only a ﬁxed number of sliding window
templates is applied, unsatisfactory regions may be produced.
B. Feature Extraction
To recognize different objects, we need to extract visual
features that can provide a semantic and robust represen-
tation. Scale-invariant feature transform [19], histograms of
oriented gradients (HOG) [20], and Haar-like [21] features are
the representative ones. This is due to the fact that these
features can produce representations associated with complex
cells in human brain [19]. However, due to the diversity of
appearances, illumination conditions, and backgrounds, it is
difﬁcult to manually design a robust feature descriptor to
perfectly describe all kinds of objects.
C. Classiﬁcation
Besides, a classiﬁer is needed to distinguish a target object
from all the other categories and to make the representations
more hierarchical, semantic, and informative for visual recog-
nition. Usually, the supported vector machine (SVM) [22],
AdaBoost [23], and deformable part-based model (DPM) [24]
are good choices. Among these classiﬁers, the DPM is a
ﬂexible model by combining object parts with deformation
cost to handle severe deformations. In DPM, with the aid
of a graphical model, carefully designed low-level features
and kinematically inspired part decompositions are combined.

II. BRIEF OVERVIEW OF DEEP LEARNING
Prior to an overview on deep learning-based object detection
approaches, we provide a review on the history of deep
learning along with an introduction on the basic architecture
and advantages of CNN.
A. History: Birth, Decline, and Prosperity
Deep models can be referred to as neural networks with
deep structures. The history of neural networks can date
back to the 1940s [36], and the original intention was to
simulate the human brain system to solve general learning
problems in a principled way. It was popular in the 1980s and
1990s with the proposal of the back-propagation algorithm
by Rumelhart et al. [37]. However, due to the overﬁtting of
training, lack of large-scale training data, limited computation
power, and insigniﬁcance in performance compared with other
machine learning tools, neural networks fell out of fashion in
the early 2000s.
Deep learning has become popular since 2006 [26], [S7],
with a breakthrough in speech recognition [38]. The recovery
of deep learning can be attributed to the following factors.
1) The emergence of large-scale annotated training data,
such as ImageNet [39], to fully exhibit its very large
learning capacity.
2) Fast development of high-performance parallel comput-
ing systems, such as GPU clusters.
3) Signiﬁcant advances in the design of network structures
and training strategies. With unsupervised and layerwise
pretraining guided by autoencoder [40] or restricted
Boltzmann machine [41], a good initialization is pro-
vided. With dropout and data augmentation, the over-
ﬁtting problem in training has been relieved [6], [42].

B. Architecture and Advantages of CNN
CNN is the most representative model of deep learning [27].
A typical CNN architecture, which is referred to as VGG16,
can be found in Fig. S1 in the supplementary material. Each
layer of CNN is known as a feature map. The feature map
of the input layer is a 3-D matrix of pixel intensities for
different color channels (e.g., RGB). The feature map of
any internal layer is an induced multichannel image, whose
“pixel” can be viewed as a speciﬁc feature. Every neu-
ron is connected with a small portion of adjacent neurons
from the previous layer (receptive ﬁeld). Different types of
transformations [6], [49], [50] can be conducted on feature
maps, such as ﬁltering and pooling. Filtering (convolution)
operation convolutes a ﬁlter matrix (learned weights) with
the values of a receptive ﬁeld of neurons and takes a non-
linear function (such as sigmoid [51], ReLU) to obtain ﬁnal
responses. Pooling operation, such as max pooling, average
pooling, L2-pooling, and local contrast normalization [52],
summarizes the responses of a receptive ﬁeld into one value
to produce more robust feature descriptions.
With an interleave between convolution and pooling, an ini-
tial feature hierarchy is constructed, which can be ﬁne-tuned
in a supervised manner by adding several fully connected (FC)
layers to adapt to different visual tasks. According to the tasks
involved, the ﬁnal layer with different activation functions [6]
is added to get a speciﬁc conditional probability for each
output neuron. The whole network can be optimized on an
objective function (e.g., mean squared error or cross-entropy
loss) via the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) method. The
typical VGG16 has totally 13 convolutional (conv) layers,
3 FC layers, 3 max-pooling layers, and a softmax classiﬁcation
layer. The conv feature maps are produced by convoluting
3*3 ﬁlter windows, and feature map resolutions are reduced
with 2 stride max-pooling layers. An arbitrary test image of the
same size as training samples can be processed with the trained
network. Rescaling or cropping operations may be needed if
different sizes are provided [6].

III. GENERIC OBJECT DETECTION
Generic object detection aims at locating and classifying
existing objects in any one image and labeling them with
rectangular BBs to show the conﬁdences of existence. The
frameworks of generic object detection methods can mainly
be categorized into two types (see Fig. 2). One follows the tra-
ditional object detection pipeline, generating region proposals
at ﬁrst and then classifying each proposal into different object
categories. The other regards object detection as a regression
or classiﬁcation problem, adopting a uniﬁed framework to
achieve ﬁnal results (categories and locations) directly. The
region proposal-based methods mainly include R-CNN [15],
spatial pyramid pooling (SPP)-net [64], Fast R-CNN [16],
Faster R-CNN [17], region-based fully convolutional network
(R-FCN) [65], feature pyramid networks (FPN)
[66], and
Mask R-CNN [67], some of which are correlated with each

deconvolutional single shot detector (DSSD) [73], and deeply
supervised object detectors (DSOD) [74]. The correlations

A B S T R A C T
Object detection is one of the most important and challenging tasks of computer vision. It has numerous ap­
plications in the fields of agriculture, defence, retail markets and manufacturing units, transportation, social 
media platforms, medical, wildlife monitoring and conservation. This survey aims to give researchers a 
comprehensive understanding of the current state of object detection algorithms. In this review, object detection 
and its different aspects have been covered in detail. This review paper starts with a quick overview of object 
detection followed by traditional and deep learning models for object detection. The section on deep learning 
models provides a comprehensive overview of one-stage and two-stage object detectors. A detailed discussion is 
given of the transformer-based detectors and lightweight networks category. Additionally, the evaluation metrics 
used for object detection methods are discussed systematically. The best object detection algorithms for different 
applications are discussed at the end of the survey. This survey is useful for beginners who want to study different 
object detection algorithms and their use in different applications.
1. Introduction
Object detection is one of the most important tasks in computer 
vision, involving the identification of visual instances of specific object 
classes within an image or complex real-world scenes. Its ability to 
identify, classify, and localize multiple objects within an image or video 
frame makes it a vital component of numerous applications. Object 
detection is crucial across industries, enabling autonomous navigation, 
security surveillance, medical imaging, retail automation, precision 
farming, and quality control in manufacturing. Recognizing objects in 
real-time, it enhances safety, efficiency, and decision-making. Ad­
vancements in AI and deep learning continue to drive its transformative 
impact, making it indispensable for the future. Due to its wide range of 
applications and recent technological advancements, this field has 
gained significant attention. The primary objective of object detection 
methods is to develop computational models that provide essential data 
for computer vision-based systems. Currently, object detection is a 
deeply researched area, both in academic studies and practical appli­
cations [17].
The Viola-Jones detector, Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG), 
and other manually constructed feature extractors formed the early 
object detection models, also referred to as traditional models. These 
models performed poorly on unknown datasets and were slow and un­
reliable. The field of visual perception transformed with the reintro­
duction of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and deep learning for 
image classification. Currently, deep learning is being used in a variety 
of computer vision applications, including semantic segmentation, 
detecting objects, image classification, and image retrieval. Lightweight 
neural networks or mobile-friendly neural networks are deep neural 
networks which are designed for mobile devices or other resource- 
limited hardware [135].
Several reviews on object detectors have been published in recent 
years [131,133,140,146–151], serving as early efforts to summarize the 
object detection models available at the time of their publication. 
However, the rapid advancements in computer vision, particularly in 
object detection, have led to the emergence of numerous enhanced deep 
learning models. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of object 
detection methodologies, encompassing traditional approaches, deep 
learning-based techniques, and their subcategories, including one-stage, 
two-stage, transformer-based, and lightweight models. It examines their 
advantages, limitations, and the evolution of network architectures, 
with a particular emphasis on the research gap in lightweight models—a

2. Overview of object detection algorithms
Object detection has emerged as a cornerstone in the field of com­
puter vision, enabling machines to identify and localize objects within 
images or videos. Over the years, numerous algorithms have been 
developed, each offering unique approaches to improve accuracy, speed, 
and scalability. Classical methods such as Viola-Jones and HOG-SVM 
laid the foundation by employing hand-crafted features and sliding 
window techniques. The advent of deep learning revolutionized object 
detection with the introduction of convolutional neural networks 
(CNNs), giving rise to modern architectures like R-CNN, SSD, and YOLO, 
which prioritize real-time performance and precision. The several

3. The need and motivation for having this survey
Object detection is a fundamental computer vision task that involves 
identifying and locating objects within an image or video. The need for 
object detection models arises from their diverse real-world applica­
tions, as well as the continuous advancements in technology that make 
these tasks possible. The motivation for doing this survey is mentioned 
below. 
• Automation: The demand for automation in diverse industries drives 
the need for object detection models, enabling machines to perceive 
and interact with their surroundings intelligently. In autonomous 
vehicles like drones, cars etc. object detection models are required to 
identify pedestrians, vehicles, road signs, and obstacles in real time 
to navigate safely [89].
• Healthcare: In medical imaging, object detection is used to locate 
tumours, lesions, and abnormalities in X-rays, CT scans and MRIs, 
aiding in diagnostic processes.
• Surveillance: Models identify faces in surveillance footage, helping 
law enforcement and security personnel monitor public spaces, 
identify suspects, or secure access points and monitor real-time video 
streams to detect suspicious activities, identify intruders, or track 
moving objects in public spaces or homes [18].
• Sports: Object detection can be used to track players, analyse their 
movements, and provide insights into game strategies by analysing 
live broadcasts.
• Threat Detection: Detecting weapons, explosives, or other dangerous 
objects in X-ray images or CCTV footage at airports, train stations, 
and other public places is critical for preventing security threats 
[19].
• Wildlife Conservation: Object detection is used in camera traps or 
drones to monitor wildlife populations and track endangered species, 
contributing to conservation efforts.
• Disaster Management: In post-disaster scenarios (e.g., earthquakes, 
floods), object detection can help locate survivors, detect damaged 
structures, and monitor affected areas [135].
• Agriculture: Precision agriculture utilizes object detection to monitor 
crop health, detect pests, and manage resources more efficiently, 
contributing to sustainable farming practices [135].
Despite the advances, there are significant challenges that motivate 
the continuous survey and development of object detection models. The 
first key challenge is achieving high-quality detection across multiple 
scales. This means detecting both large and small objects simultaneously 
with the same model, which remains a difficult task. Secondly, handling 
complex scenes which includes detecting objects in crowded or cluttered 
environments, such as traffic scenes, supermarkets, or gatherings, is 
complex and the third challenge is to reduce false positives/negatives, 
while object detection models have become more accurate, reducing the 
rates of false positives (incorrect detections) and false negatives (missed 
detections) is still a priority, especially in high-stakes applications like 
healthcare or autonomous driving. The need for object detection models 
is driven by a wide array of practical applications, ranging from auto­
mation and real-time analysis to safety, security, and societal benefits. 
The motivation for developing increasingly sophisticated and efficient 
models lies in addressing the challenges of real-world environments, 
enabling AI systems to perceive and interact with the world more 
effectively [135]. Continuous advancements in machine learning and 
deep learning architectures are essential to meet these growing 
demands.
